Lung injury is closely associated with the heterogeneity, severity, mortality, and prognosis of various respiratory diseases. Effective monitoring of lung injury is crucial for the optimal management and improved outcomes of patients with lung diseases. This review describes acute and chronic respiratory diseases characterized by significant lung injury and current clinical tools for assessing lung health. Furthermore, we summarized the mechanisms of lung cell death observed in these diseases and highlighted recently identified biomarkers in the plasma indicative of injury to specific cell types and scaffold structure in the lung. Last, we propose an artificial intelligence-driven lung injury monitoring model to assess disease severity, and predict mortality and prognosis, aiming to achieve precision and personalized medicine. Keywords Biomarkers Respiratory disease Artificial intelligence Inflammation Infections Tianjin Key Medical Discipline (Specialty) Construction Project TJYXZDXK-063B, TJYXZDXK-067C TJYXZDXK-063B, TJYXZDXK-067C Li Li Chen Huaiyong http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100002855 Ministry of Science and Technology of the People's Republic of China 2023YFC3502605 Chen Huaiyong http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100001809 National Natural Science Foundation of China 82070001 Chen Huaiyong Natural Science Foundation of Tianjin City in China 21JCZDJC00430 Chen Huaiyong issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2024 Introduction Acute and chronic lung diseases pose significant health challenges and economic burdens, impacting both severity and prognosis primarily through lung injury. Despite clinical focus on overall lung alterations, diagnosis relies heavily on symptomatic, morphological, and functional assessments. These include imaging for indirect lung morphology observation, lung function tests, arterial blood gas analysis, and non-invasive oxygen saturation measurements to assess gas exchange [ 1 , 2 ]. Pathological examinations aid in disease elucidation but often lack specificity regarding injury location, affected cell types, and injury extent. This limitation complicates the development of precise, personalized treatment strategies. Lung injury encompasses damage to epithelial and endothelial cells, along with the extracellular scaffold supporting these cells. This damage triggers the release of cellular proteins, activating resident inflammatory cells, increasing vascular permeability, and promoting inflammatory cell infiltration into the lungs. While essential for immune defense, inflammatory cells can exacerbate cellular damage. Circulating proteins from damaged cells offer a means to precisely monitor lung cellular and structural damage by analyzing cell-specific protein expression levels in serum. Concurrent detection of oxidative irritants or cytokines contributing to lung cell damage further enhances diagnostic capabilities. Recent advancements in omics technologies have significantly improved the identification of lung injury biomarkers [ 3 ]. This review will summarize lung injury characteristics across common lung diseases, elucidate molecular mechanisms of injury, and catalog specific serum biomarkers indicative of inflammatory, oxidative, epithelial, endothelial, and extracellular scaffold damage in the lung. Pathogenesis and biomarkers of lung remodeling and fibrosis are not the focus of this review, as these topics have been comprehensively covered in recent literature [ 3 – 7 ]. Additionally, it will propose an integrated lung injury evaluation platform, aiming to amalgamate these biomarkers with clinical indicators and demographic data, utilizing artificial intelligence to accurately assess disease severity, predict patient outcomes, and determine long-term prognosis. Respiratory diseases with lung injury In acute respiratory infections, various viral and bacterial pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, Streptococcus pneumoniae , and Mycobacterium tuberculosis lead to lung injury by targeting specific cell types within the lung (Fig. 1 ). Respiratory viruses invade epithelial cells and endothelial cells, triggering cell death mechanisms like apoptosis, pyroptosis, or necrosis. This process releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, exacerbating inflammation and compromising the airway and air-blood barrier integrity. Inflammatory responses upregulate leukocyte adhesion molecules, promoting immune cell accumulation and worsening lung function. Bacterial infections cause pneumonia characterized by pulmonary edema, inflammatory exudates, and recruitment of immune cells, which further disrupts the air-blood barrier and leads to systemic infection in severe cases [ 8 ]. Chronic infections may lead to bronchiectasis and irreversible airway dilation. Neutrophils, macrophages, and eosinophils predominate in lung inflammation, generating ROS, cytokines, and NETs that contribute to ongoing lung scaffold damage and mucus hypersecretion [ 9 ]. Apoptosis of inflammatory cells and epithelial cells like ciliated and club cells worsens airway integrity, perpetuating the disease cycle. In chronic lung disease such as asthma, allergen or irritant-induced inflammation causes airway epithelial shedding, mucin production, and remodeling. The epithelial layer is compromised, with increased apoptosis of ciliated cells and impaired repair processes, leading to airway hyperresponsiveness (Fig. 1 ). Eosinophil-mediated injury of club cells contributes to disease severity of asthma [ 10 , 11 ]. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) encompasses bronchitis, fibrosis and emphysema attributing to three variant lung epithelial progenitor respectively, is also found with apoptosis of club cells, ciliated cells, AT1 cells, AT2 cells, and endothelial cells [ 12 ]. Inflammatory cells release neutrophil elastase and matrix metalloproteinase (MMPs), disrupting the lung's proteinase/anti-proteinase balance and causing the degradation of lung elastin and connective tissue [ 13 ]. ECM remodeling and altered collagen deposition further contribute to lung function decline. Interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and connective tissue disease-associated ILD (CTD-ILD) involve fibroblast proliferation, ECM deposition, and myofibroblast differentiation. TGF-β signaling upregulation drives fibrogenesis, leading to irreversible lung fibrosis, AT1 and AT2 cell loss, and alveolar epithelial stem cell dysfunction [ 14 ]. These changes exacerbate lung injury, compromising respiratory function and prognosis in affected individuals. Clinical markers indicative of lung injury Symptoms such as cough with phlegm suggest upper airway involvement, common in infections, bronchitis, and pneumonia, while chest tightness, pain, and shortness of breath indicate alveolar issues like fluid accumulation or pulmonary embolism [ 15 ]. Abnormal breath sounds like wheezes indicate airway obstruction (e.g., asthma), while crackles signify fluid or secretion in airways (e.g., bronchitis, pneumonia). Velcro crackles denote diffuse interstitial pulmonary fibrosis [ 16 ]. Lung percussion reveals resonant sounds normally, hyperresonance in emphysema, and dullness in conditions like pleural effusion [ 17 ]. Imaging techniques like X-rays and CT scans show low attenuation in emphysema and high attenuation in inflammatory states, consolidation, or general interstitial lung abnormalities [ 18 , 19 ]. Lung function tests detect obstructive patterns (e.g., reduced FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio) and restrictive patterns (e.g., reduced lung capacities), while blood gas analysis assesses gas exchange impairments like low PaO 2 indicating ventilation issues and elevated PaCO 2 indicating gas exchange problems [ 20 ]. OI values < 300 mmHg suggest acute lung injury, < 100 mmHg may indicate ARDS. These assessments provide insights into lung conditions but do not fully capture cellular injury or predict disease outcomes, highlighting the need for comprehensive monitoring strategies.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Lung injury in acute and chronic respiratory diseases; cell death induced by various agents and its associated biomarkers; diverse lung diseases, endothelial damage, inflammation, tissue injury; respiratory diseases and lung injury.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Lung injury in acute and chronic respiratory diseases involves damage to epithelial and endothelial cells and the extracellular scaffold, leading to the release of cellular proteins, activation of inflammatory cells, increased vascular permeability, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Cell death mechanisms include apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and necroptosis, triggered by viral (e.g., SARS-CoV-2, RSV) and bacterial infections (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis), as well as oxidative stress. Inflammatory cells (neutrophils, macrophages, eosinophils) generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), cytokines (e.g., TNF-"alpha, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1"beta, IL-18), and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), exacerbating cellular damage and promoting pro-inflammatory responses, vascular permeability, and tissue disruption. In COPD, increased neutrophil elastase and matrix metalloproteinase (MMPs) disrupt the proteinase/anti-proteinase balance, degrading lung elastin and connective tissue. In Interstitial Lung Diseases (ILDs), TGF-"beta signaling drives fibrogenesis, leading to fibroblast proliferation, extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, and myofibroblast differentiation. Biomarkers such as CCSP are released from injured club cells, sRAGE from injured AT1 cells, and SP-D from injured AT2 cells. Endothelial damage leads to the release of EMPs, Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), Endothelin-1 (ET-1), Von Willebrand Factor (VWF), Selectins, Cell Adhesion Molecules, and components of the endothelial glycocalyx (syndecan-1, hyaluronic acid, heparan sulfate). Soluble thrombomodulin (sTM) and Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) reflect coagulation and anti-coagulation imbalances. Laminin and Endostatin indicate basement membrane fragmentation and impaired epithelial repair. MMPs and TIMPs regulate ECM remodeling. Osteopontin (OPN) promotes inflammation and fibrosis. Fas/FasL signaling is involved in apoptosis, and S100A8/S100A9 are DAMPs inducing apoptosis. Oxidative stress from ROS causes lung tissue damage. Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) are released upon cellular injury, death, or renewal. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) and various microRNAs (e.g., miR-29a-3p, miR-150, miR-1, miR-122) and lncRNAs mediate intercellular communication and are implicated in disease severity. Biomarker expression is intricately regulated and influenced by disease complexity and comorbidities, reflecting the heterogeneity of respiratory diseases and the location/extent of lung injury.
related_biomarkers: Enzyme antioxidants (glutathione, glutathione peroxidase, superoxide dismutase)

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Oxygenation Index (OI) values provide an indication of acute lung injury severity: OI values less than 300 mmHg suggest acute lung injury, while values less than 100 mmHg may indicate Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). Elevated CK-18 levels in BALF correlate with ARDS severity. Plasma CYFRA21-1 levels are higher in severe ARDS and COVID-19 patients and associate with systemic sclerosis-ILD severity. Plasma TNF-"alpha levels are higher in intensive care (ICU) patients with COVID-19 than non-ICU patients. Mild COVID-19 cases exhibit increased sFas levels, while severe cases show lower levels relative to both control and mild COVID-19. Elevated plasma endostatin levels correlate with mortality rates in severe COVID-19 cases. Plasma S100A9/S100A8 levels correlate with disease severity of COVID-19. IL-1"beta, IL-6, and IL-8 levels correlate with the severity of COVID-19 and IPF. Serum ROS levels are negatively correlated with lung function parameters in COPD patients. A combination of ferritin and KL-6 showed significantly greater predictive efficacy for progression to severe ARDS compared to any individual biomarker. These findings indicate a correlation between biomarker levels and disease intensity/severity, but no explicit dose-response experiment for a single intervention is described.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Traditional pathological examinations often lack specificity regarding injury location, affected cell types, and injury extent. However, analyzing cell-specific protein expression levels in serum from circulating proteins released by damaged cells offers a means to precisely monitor lung cellular and structural damage. sRAGE is a disease-specific marker for AT1 cell injury, and CCSP is specifically expressed by club cells. KL-6 shows a large effect size in identifying high-risk patients. EMPs reflect severe endothelial damage and vascular dysfunction, while Ang-2 indicates disrupted endothelial barrier function. Shedding of glycocalyx components (syndecan-1, hyaluronic acid, heparan sulfate) predicts severe ARDS, COPD exacerbations, IPF, or CTD-ILD. ET-1 correlates with impaired lung function, and VWF is indicative of vascular damage and immune cell extravasation. sTM is known for its anti-inflammatory and anticoagulant properties. PAI-1 promotes thrombus formation. Laminin indicates sustained epithelial and scaffold injury and suggests impaired epithelial repair. Endostatin is implicated in endothelial damage. MMPs degrade ECM components, contributing to tissue damage, while TIMP-1 levels are linked to fibrosis. OPN promotes inflammation, tissue injury, and fibrosis. IL-18 increases vascular permeability, leading to tissue damage and microthrombus formation. cfDNA, mtDNA, and EVs are derived from cellular injury/death or mediate intercellular communication. The predictive performance of individual biomarkers (CCSP, SP-D, KL-6) for ARDS mortality was suboptimal, with SP-D having the lowest predictive ability. In contrast, the combination of ferritin and KL-6 showed significantly greater predictive efficacy for progression to severe ARDS, suggesting improved specificity through combined analysis.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Patients with acute and chronic respiratory diseases, including those with acute respiratory infections, asthma, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), Interstitial Lung Diseases (ILDs), ARDS, COVID-19, sarcoidosis, pulmonary fibrosis, pediatric ARDS, adult ARDS, IPF, A/H1N1 infections, systemic sclerosis-ILD, septic ARDS, asthma exacerbations, connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD), rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD), and ICU patients.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Lung injury is closely associated with the heterogeneity, severity, mortality, and prognosis of various respiratory diseases, posing significant health challenges and economic burdens. It leads to impaired gas exchange, irreversible lung fibrosis, decline in lung function, and worsened airway integrity. Biomarkers predict mortality rates (e.g., CCSP in ARDS, SP-D in A/H1N1), indicate specific cell injury (e.g., sRAGE for AT1, KL-6 for AT2), and correlate with disease severity (e.g., CRTAC-1 in severe COVID-19, CK18/CYFRA 21-1 in ARDS). CECs and EMPs reflect severe endothelial damage and vascular dysfunction, with implications for adverse outcomes like microthrombus formation and disseminated intravascular coagulation. These biomarkers collectively reflect severe endothelial damage, vascular dysfunction, disrupted endothelial barrier function, impaired lung function, vascular damage, immune cell extravasation, higher mortality rates, adverse outcomes, thrombus formation, sustained epithelial and scaffold injury, impaired epithelial repair, inflammation, tissue injury, apoptosis, dysregulated immune responses, increased vascular permeability, and lung tissue damage. Reduced sphingosine-1-phosphate correlates with ARDS prognosis. Improved diagnostic accuracy, personalized treatment plans, streamlined workflows, and enhanced patient management are critical for predicting the incidence of severity and mortality risk, enabling timely interventions to avoid severe progression. For IPF, an epithelial injury cluster was linked to the highest risk of mortality and lung function decline. Overall, these markers provide insights into disease mechanisms and may guide targeted therapies aimed at preserving lung structure and improving patient outcomes.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility is highlighted for assessing disease severity (e.g., OI < 300 mmHg for ALI; OI < 100 mmHg for ARDS) and identifying specific injuries (e.g., sRAGE for AT1 cell injury, KL-6 for AT2 cell damage, CK18/CYFRA 21-1 for epithelial cell death, CECs/EMPs for endothelial injury), especially when using AI models and biomarker combinations. Prognostic utility is demonstrated for predicting patient outcomes and long-term prognosis, including ARDS mortality (e.g., CCSP, SP-D), A/H1N1 mortality risk, pediatric ARDS severity (SP-D), and identifying high-risk patients (KL-6). Adverse risks indicated include cytokine storms, inflammation, microthrombus formation, disseminated intravascular coagulation, increased pulmonary permeability associated with cytokine-induced cell death, and the highest risk of mortality for IPF epithelial injury clusters. Improved monitoring is crucial for optimal management, achieving precision and personalized medicine, and AI-directed monitoring can reduce mortality and severe progression.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Current clinical tools (imaging, lung function tests, blood gas analysis, pathological examinations) often lack specificity and do not fully capture cellular injury or predict disease outcomes. Traditional methods of integrating biomarkers with clinical examinations have not achieved breakthroughs in lung injury monitoring. The predictive performance of individual biomarkers (CCSP, SP-D, KL-6) for ARDS mortality was suboptimal, with SP-D having the lowest predictive ability, indicating that single biomarkers may be inadequate due to disease complexity and intricate regulation of expression. However, recent advancements in omics technologies have significantly improved biomarker identification. KL-6 has the largest effect size in identifying high-risk patients, and sRAGE is a disease-specific marker for AT1 cell injury. The correlation of CK18 with ARDS severity and CYFRA21-1 with severe ARDS/COVID-19 severity supports their reliability. Endothelial glycocalyx component levels, G2F decrease in survivors, sTM, endostatin, OPN, S100A9/S100A8, ROS, and miR-122 all show correlations with disease severity, outcomes, or prognosis, serving as vital indicators of endothelial dysfunction and injury. Several biomarkers are also effective in monitoring oxidative stress.
recommended_alternatives: Artificial intelligence-driven lung injury monitoring model
Integrated lung injury evaluation platform (amalgamating biomarkers with clinical indicators and demographic data)
Combination of ferritin and KL-6 (for predicting severe ARDS progression)
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (for integrating diverse data like laboratory tests, imaging, pathological results, and patient demographics)
Peripheral blood-based laboratory tests and biomarker identification (preferred over invasive BALF samples)
Emerging soluble factors involved in lung epithelial and endothelial cell repair and regeneration
Multi-omics metabolic profiling (including epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics) for future comprehensive biomarker discovery
